newsitem.title: USA: US manufacturing, construction soften; economy steady.
newsitem.headline: US manufacturing, construction soften; economy steady.

text.p: The nation's busy manufacturing industries eased a notch in June, purchasing managers reported on Tuesday, soothing edgy markets as Federal Reserve policy-makers began meeting to chart the course of interest rates.

The downturn in the closely watched Purchasing Managers' Index to 55.7 percent from 57.1 percent in May -- accompanied by falling prices -- complemented a separate Commerce Department report that May construction spending had faltered.

Yet a third report, from the private Conference Board in New York, showed little or no likelihood of a downturn developing as the forward-looking Index of Leading Indicators rebounded 0.3 percent in May after a 0.1 percent April fall.

Analysts said the reports showed the economy slowing on its own from a blistering 5.9 percent annual rate of growth in the first quarter, making it unlikely the central bank will boost interest rates at its two-day meeting's conclusion on Wednesday.

But there were also at least the seeds of a future spending pickup in the reports, which may keep pressure on members of the Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-making body, at future meetings. Stock and bond prices surged on the reports, especially from the purchasing managers, the front-line executives buying products ranging from paper to steel for industry.
"What we have is an economy that is cooling off, but cooling off to a healthy pace of growth rather than an absurd pace," said economist Kevin Harris of MCM MoneyWatch in New York.

The National Association of Purchasing Management said its production index component decreased only from 57.0 percent to 56.0 percent, while its new orders measure fell from 64.2 percent to 62.0 percent. Prices eased for a third straight month.

"It's an extraordinary set of circumstances," Harris said. "We can have soft prices and still get strong growth" in the manufacturing sector. Only three industries -- printing and publishing, chemicals, and industrial and commercial equipment, including computers -- said prices were up in June from May.

The construction spending report showed a sharp turnaround in May, with outlays dropping 1.8 percent after rising by 0.3 percent in April. Both government and private-sector projects were scaled back as spending fell at the sharpest rate in more than three years, since a 3 percent drop in January 1994.

Somewhat surprisingly, public, or government-sponsored, construction spending dropped 5.9 percent in May to $131.3 billion a year -- the steepest decrease since a 6.1 percent plunge in January 1994 -- after a 1.1 percent drop in April.

"Filled state and local coffers should be bringing forth efforts to rebuild infrastructure and schools," said Joel Naroff, Philadelphia-based economist for First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C. He added there was a possibility of snapback in government spending in the summer.
Spending weakened during May on highways and streets, water treatment plants and hospitals and schools.
On the private-sector side, construction spending was down 0.5 percent overall to a rate of $453.7 billion in May after a 0.7 percent increase in April.

The Conference Board's May leading index, designed to forecast economic trends six to nine months ahead, reinforced the impression of steady growth ahead in the seventh year of expansion from the 1990-91 recession.

Six of its 10 separate measures of economic activity were higher in May than in April. The biggest contributor to the May advance was surging stock prices, which put more wealth in consumers' accounts and pocketbooks for future spending.
Soaring levels of consumer optimism, fueled by plentiful jobs and rising incomes, also helped push the index up in May and could portend more vigorous consumer spending in the summer and fall.
